extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, litigators, judges, and IP counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and principles for allocating responsibility between judge and jury for interpreting patent claims and related documentary terms in U.S. patent litigation. Explains historical test, functional considerations, evidentiary role of experts, and policy reasons for judicial construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of a patent claim is a question of law for the court
rubrics_metrics.description: "The construction of a patent, including terms of art within its claim, is exclusively within the province of the court."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court holds claim construction is a legal determination for the judge (not the jury). The opinion affirms that interpreting the words in the claim to determine scope is a judicial function and must be decided as a matter of law. (See also Winans v. Denmead: first issue is construing the letters-patent — question of law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between claim construction (law) and infringement (fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first is a question of law, to be determined by the court, construing the letters-patent... The second is a question of fact, to be submitted to a jury."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent cases have two separable elements: (1) construing the patent (judge) and (2) determining whether a defendant's product/process falls within that construction (jury on infringement). Courts must 'lay down to the jury the law which should govern them' on factual issues once construction is judicially determined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh Amendment historical test for jury rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The Seventh Amendment preserves the right which existed under the English common law when the Amendment was adopted; ask whether the cause of action was tried at law then or is analogous to one that was.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To decide whether a particular trial issue must be submitted to a jury, compare the modern cause of action to 18th-century English causes of action; if no direct antecedent exists, seek the best available analogy to determine whether the issue is an essential incident of the jury-trial right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where no direct antecedent exists, compare to earlier practices and draw best analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: When the old practice provides no clear answer, the modern practice should be compared to earlier practices whose allocation to court or jury is known, and the best analogy drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precedent and analogical reasoning (Granfinanciera, Tull) to classify 'mongrel' practices. The Court compares modern claim construction to historical practices (e.g., construction of specifications, land patents) to determine allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable; claims define the scope of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent contains a specification describing the invention 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the same.' 35 U.S.C. §112. Claims 'particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification (enablement/description) and claims (particular pointing-out) serve different functions. Claims 'define the scope of a patent grant' and must be construed to determine what is covered. Claims cover machines, manufactures, compositions, or processes — not abstract functions or scientific explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges are better positioned than juries to construe technical patent terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge, from his training and discipline, is more likely to give a proper interpretation to highly technical patents than a jury and is in a better position to ascertain whether an expert's proposed definition fully comports with the instrument as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional considerations favor judicial construction: judges have training in interpreting documents, can perform sophisticated analysis of the patent 'as a whole,' ensure internal coherence between claims and specification, and apply specialized doctrines developed by courts and the Patent Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony may inform the court but does not supplant judicial interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where technical terms are used... the testimony of witnesses may be received upon these subjects... But in the actual interpretation of the patent the court proceeds upon its own responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may and should consider expert evidence to understand technical terms or the 'outward embodiment' of inventions, but the court retains ultimate interpretive responsibility and is not obliged to 'blindly follow' expert testimony. Expert credibility may inform the court's analysis but typically becomes part of the broader document-based construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity in treatment of patents favors judicial allocation of claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The need for uniformity in the treatment of a given patent favors allocation of construction issues to the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial construction promotes intrajurisdictional and interjurisdictional predictability (stare decisis, Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit) and reduces a 'zone of uncertainty' that would otherwise discourage innovation and experimentation if claim meaning varied by jury across courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish documentary construction from 'evidence in pais' (physical identity issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bischoff held that it is not the construction of the instrument, but the character of the thing invented (its outward embodiment), which may be sought by evidence in pais and presented to a jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the dispute concerns the physical identity or characteristics of an accused device (outward embodiment), expert evidence to the jury on identity/diversity is appropriate. By contrast, the legal interpretation of documentary terms (the claim language) remains for the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility disputes alone are rarely sufficient to convert construction into a jury issue
rubrics_metrics.description: There could be a case in which a simple credibility judgment would suffice to choose between experts... But our own experience with document construction leaves us doubtful that trial courts will run into many cases like that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when experts offer competing meanings, courts expect that resolution typically requires sophisticated analysis of the patent as a whole, subsuming credibility into legal interpretation. Simple credibility determinations are exceptional and do not generally warrant submission of claim construction to a jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical practice indicates judges, not juries, construed patent specifications and written instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Early case reports and treatises show judges, rather than jurors, ordinarily construed written documents and specifications in patent cases; no established 18th-century jury practice supports plenary jury interpretation of patent terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court cites English and early American precedent (e.g., Bovill v. Moore; Winans decisions) and commentary to support judicial primacy in document interpretation. Historical ambiguity or later exceptions (Neilson) do not displace the general rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public policy: clarity of patent limits is essential for innovation and public notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The limits of a patent must be known for the protection of the patentee, the encouragement of the inventive genius of others and the assurance that the subject of the patent will be dedicated ultimately to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity about claim scope creates a 'zone of uncertainty' that discourages invention. Judicially consistent claim construction helps provide notice to the public and protect both patentees and potential innovators; this policy supports treating construction as a legal issue.
